buffer.text: Richpanel helps companies automate 50% of support in 30 days | OpenAI OpenAI November 23, 2026 Startup Richpanel helps companies automate 50% of support in 30 days Richpanel uses GPT‑6 Astra and GPT‑6.1 Sol to equip its AI support agents with tools and procedures, and GPT‑6 Luna for their conversations. Start building with OpenAI Company size: Startup Region: Asia-Pacific & Oceania Industry: Technology Products: API Share Beyond knowing how to answer a customer’s request, AI support agents need to be able to execute a solution. And for that, they need access to the right tools and instructions. According to Richpanel CEO Amit RG, human support agents can use 20 or 30 tools to serve a customer, and the procedures they follow may never have been written down. Richpanel ⁠ (opens in a new window) solves that using OpenAI models to both set up the tools and procedures AI support agents need to act and handle customer conversations. “The intelligence is no longer the bottleneck. It’s everything around it.” —Amit RG, CEO, Richpanel Building the tools and procedures for AI support Deploying a support agent often requires a forward-deployed engineer to connect the agent to a customer’s systems and define how it should work. Amit saw that many companies didn’t have engineers to spare and asked himself, “What if that forward-deployed engineer itself was an AI agent?” So Richpanel built it: an AI manager to handle agent setup. Customers began calling it Boss AI. It writes procedures and defines how Richpanel’s frontline support agent, copilot, and quality-assurance agent call the tools they need. Richpanel uses GPT‑6 Astra and GPT‑6.1 Sol for Boss AI, prioritizing accuracy when building the tools and procedures its other agents will follow. Balancing intelligence and cost across support operations Richpanel designs the frontline agent to handle hundreds of thousands of conversations, making the cost of each interaction an important part of model selection. It uses GPT‑6 Luna and other OpenAI models for that work. Amit says Richpanel takes the same approach to its copilot and quality-assurance agents. “What matters is a balance of cost and intelligence,” Amit says. Richpanel’s customers may already use low-cost outsourced support. Automating their operations has to make financial sense against that starting point. Amit credits OpenAI with making models available that can handle long context and longer tasks while remaining cost efficient. Richpanel can use deeper reasoning to prepare its support agents and more economical models to run the conversations that follow. “OpenAI models can run these long-context, longer-horizon tasks while still being very cost efficient.” —Amit RG, CEO, Richpanel Increasing contact center automation and customer satisfaction At the time of the October 2026 interview, Amit said Richpanel had completed approximately 300 AI customer-support deployments over the previous six months. The company guarantees customers a 50% automation rate within the first 30 days or their money back. Amit says it met that commitment across all of those deployments, adding, “In each of the cases, the AI is beating human support agents when it comes to customer satisfaction.” OpenAI <3 startups Join the community Start building (opens in a new window) Get OpenAI for Business updates Product updates, practical guides, upcoming events, and more. buffer.title: Finding faster quantum algorithms with agents and formal verification
buffer.text: Finding faster quantum algorithms with agents and formal verification â Google DeepMind Skip to main content November 23, 2026 Science Finding faster quantum algorithms with agents and formal verification Sergey Shirobokov, Ben Jaderberg and Ryan Babbush Read the paper Share How using agent teams and formal verification can improve quantum algorithms for modelling fusion energy, chemistry and enzymes Quantum computers could soon solve problems beyond the reach of classical supercomputers. However, there is a catch: even when using the best quantum algorithms, some important applications still require more resources than early quantum hardware will be able to support. In a new paper , we used teams of Gemini 4 agents to improve well-known quantum algorithms, creating highly efficient quantum circuits. These optimized circuits, which are instructions for how a quantum computer should carry out an algorithm, could one day help us run simulations that solve complex scientific challenges, from fusion energy to drug design. To help the community build on this work, we are open-sourcing our Lean library , problem specifications, and verified solutions on GitHub. Because we cannot test resource-intensive quantum circuits on classical computers or today's small quantum processors, we have to prove that they work mathematically. Our agent teams proved each result using Lean, a formal theorem prover. Your browser does not support the video tag. Your browser does not support the video tag. Improving quantum algorithms using agentic teams For each problem, we tasked separate, independent agent teams with finding algorithmic improvements. These ideas were then verified with Lean, before entering a shared notebook. Every four hours, agents from each team met at a virtual conference to trade, debate and compare ideas. As teams produced more effective ideas over time, the computational cost gradually fell until the experiment finished. We chose to focus on applications that could one day impact some of humanityâs greatest challenges, such as clean energy and drug design, but our method is not limited to these problem areas. We found a quantum circuit that helps calculate an important property of inertial confinement fusion, a fusion reaction method that uses lasers to compress hydrogen fuel until ignition. Our agent teams cut the required computing cost (a metric that combines required qubits and operations) by 11.8Ã, and lowered required memory from 5,650 to 4,338 error-corrected qubits . The agents also reduced costs for simulating molecules in drug metabolism and certain photochemical reactions, which are complex reactions that are difficult for classical computers to simulate. For a common light-sensitive molecule, the agent teams made quantum simulation 8Ã cheaper, simplifying how the algorithm tracks particle positions and electric forces. For Cytochrome P450, an enzyme that breaks down most human medicines and is important for drug design, they found a 2.5Ã improvement and lowered memory from 481 to 333 qubits, by replacing bulky memory lookups. We also improved a fundamental quantum algorithm and a widely used arithmetic building block. We found a 2.57x speedup for a specific implementation of Grover's algorithm, a foundational quantum operation that searches through an unsorted list, and a 290x speedup for arcsin, a common routine that is used by many other quantum algorithms to load numbers into quantum states. Running these algorithms in scientific simulations would still demand more computational resources than the first error-corrected quantum computers are likely to provide, but these improvements are significant. We are also excited by the way in which we found them. We built a new, open-source library , in Lean for quantum algorithms which could be used by teams of collaborating agents, so their ideas were backed by mathematical correctness guarantees. We could then set the research direction by specifying the problems for our agent teams and supervise their progress. Our knowledge of quantum algorithms, combined with the way we set up our agent teams, led to real scientific results. The same approach could also accelerate other aspects of quantum computing research, and scientific discovery more broadly. Proof-checked AI search compresses work that once took years of manual design, empowering researchers to focus on choosing problems and interpreting results. buffer.title: RoboTrack: Point tracking for real-world robotic manipulation
buffer.text: RoboTrack: Point tracking for real-world robotic manipulation Back to Articles RoboTrack: Point tracking for real-world robotic manipulation Enterprise Article Published November 23, 2026 Upvote 4 Kyle Wiggers Ai2Comms Follow allenai 🤖 Models | 📄 Tech Report | 📊 Data | 💻 Code | 🌐 Project Page | 📈 Benchmark Deploying robots in real-world settings requires reliable perception throughout an interaction. To pick something up, a robot needs to follow the positions of its gripper and the object as they move. In a laboratory, a robot handling a pipette must keep track of its tip while aligning it with the opening of a tube. These tasks become harder when nearby objects clutter the view, the gripper obscures the object being handled, or the viewing angle changes. One way to help robots follow these interactions is to track specific locations on the objects they handle. This is the idea behind point tracking . Given a location in one video frame, a tracker estimates where that same point appears in subsequent frames, when it is occluded, and where it reappears. These trajectories can help robots learn from demonstrations, plan and guide movements, and model how objects respond to actions. Robotics systems often rely on off-the-shelf trackers to automatically annotate motion in videos and provide feedback during execution. And current trackers score well on established robotics benchmarks, suggesting they could be ready for wider use in real-world systems. We wanted to see whether those results hold up across the varied scenes, viewpoints, and object interactions robots encounter in practice. We introduce RoboTrack , a benchmark and training data suite for point tracking in robotic manipulation. RoboTrack-Bench contains 307 human-annotated videos from DROID, Ego-Exo4D, MolmoAct 2 , and EgoVerse, covering different robots and human hands, cluttered scenes, and first- and third-person viewpoints. To study how training data affects tracking in these settings, we also extend MolmoSpaces , Ai2’s simulation ecosystem for robot learning, to generate dense point tracks from simulated robot manipulation trajectories. This pipeline produces RoboTrack-15M , a new synthetic training dataset targeted toward robotic manipulation. RoboTrack is a benchmark and training data suite for point tracking in robotic manipulation. Built on MolmoSpaces, RoboTrack-15M (top-left) generates point tracks for training. Training with this simulated data improves tracking on real manipulation footage. RoboTrack-Bench (top-right) provides human-annotated point tracks in real manipulation videos. Our evaluations show that leading trackers score much lower on RoboTrack-Bench than on existing robotics benchmarks. Adding RoboTrack-15M to an existing tracker’s training improves performance on real manipulation video, with gains extending to other tracking benchmarks. We bring these pieces together on a real robot, using the resulting tracker to help guide pipette handling in wet-lab tasks. Today, we’re releasing both RoboTrack components and two new point tracking models: RoboTracker and RoboTracker-Warp . RoboTracker is a fine-tuned AllTracker model using our techniques and data, while RoboTracker-Warp is trained from CoWTracker. Both models improve average AJ across the three robotics benchmarks compared with their respective released baselines, and RoboTracker-Warp achieves state-of-the-art performance on four out of the five benchmarks we evaluated. We’re also releasing our paper describing the work and evaluation results. RoboTrack-Bench: A benchmark for point-tracking in real-world manipulation RoboTrack-Bench at a glance. Examples from each source dataset (307 clips and 2,522 human-verified tracks in total). MolmoAct 2 and EgoVerse show one embodiment per panel. DROID and EgoExo4D show synchronized ego (top) and exo (bottom) views. RoboTrack-Bench expands evaluation beyond controlled tabletop setups. It contains 307 videos from DROID, Ego-Exo4D, MolmoAct 2, and EgoVerse, annotated with a total of 2,522 point tracks. The videos show robots and human hands manipulating objects across cluttered scenes and first- and third-person viewpoints. Small objects can be difficult to follow against a busy background, and grippers often hide the objects they hold. Every track in RoboTrack-Bench is annotated and verified by humans. We ask annotators to prioritize points that move or become occluded rather than the many static background points in robot videos. Following the TAP-Vid annotation approach, annotators use motion estimates to help trace each point through a video. They label each track as belonging to a robot or human body, a manipulated object, or a static object to support future analysis of performance on each group. A second group of annotators checks every track frame by frame before it’s included in our curated data. To support research in multi-view pointing, correspondence, and tracking, RoboTrack-Bench contains a subset of 33 video pairs that were recorded simultaneously from two cameras. We annotate the same physical points in both views, synchronized across frames, connecting different views of the same interaction. Point trackers struggle on real-world manipulation We evaluated four leading trackers – CoTracker3, BootsTAPNext, AllTracker, and CoWTracker – on RoboTrack-Bench and four other benchmarks: RoboTAP (real-world tabletop manipulation), RGB-Stacking (simulated manipulation), and DAVIS and Kinetics (general video). We report Average Jaccard (AJ), which measures tracking accuracy and visibility prediction; higher scores are better. RoboTrack-Bench is harder than existing robot benchmarks . Every final tracker we evaluated scores lower on RoboTrack-Bench than on RoboTAP, the only other real-video robotics benchmark. Their score drops by 3.0 to 6.6 AJ. Even the strongest off-the-shelf tracker, CoWTracker, drops from 70.5 AJ on RoboTAP to 63.9 on RoboTrack-Bench. The drop holds across models despite their different architectures and training data, indicating RoboTrack-Bench identifies weaknesses across multiple trackers. RGB-Stacking rewards synthetic training more than real-world ability. BootsTAPNext is TAPNext trained further on 15 million real videos. That extra real-world training raises its RoboTrack-Bench score by 5.1 AJ (55.1 to 60.2), but lowers its RGB-Stacking score by 9.5 AJ (75.0 to 65.5). RGB-Stacking is built from simulated block stacking, and it ranks the Kubric-only model higher, while real manipulation video ranks them the other way around. A lead on the older benchmarks does not carry over. CoWTracker leads CoTracker3 by 4.7 AJ on RoboTAP, but by only 2.1 AJ on RoboTrack-Bench. AllTracker’s 2.7-point lead over CoTracker3 on RoboTAP shrinks to 0.8. BootsTAPNext, the strongest model on DAVIS, falls 3.7 AJ behind CoWTracker on RoboTrack-Bench and even trails the Kubric-only AllTracker (60.2 vs 61.4 AJ), despite its training on 15 million real videos. These results suggest that existing benchmarks give an incomplete picture of tracking performance in real-world manipulation. Evaluating on more varied scenes reveals difficulties shared by all four trackers and changes how their strengths compare. Note: Each tracker runs with its authors’ settings and is all scored in the same way. Our AllTracker scores differ slightly from the published ones because we fixed a scoring bug in its released evaluation code. Additionally, we evaluate RoboTAP and Kinetics on all annotated points rather than following AllTracker’s protocol. See our paper for full evaluation protocols. RoboTrack-15M: Simulation data from MolmoSpaces Why do these trackers struggle with real-world manipulation? Many trackers train on synthetic videos generated with Kubric , which shows objects tossed into a scene. These provide examples of motion and occlusion, but don’t focus on robots grasping and moving objects. We wanted to test whether adding trajectories from these interactions could improve tracking on real manipulation videos. This is where MolmoSpaces comes in—our robotic simulation environment at Ai2. We extend its existing manipulation simulations to generate dense point tracks on the robot and the objects it handles. In each episode, a simulated robot arm picks up an everyday object, such as a cup, a plate, or a block. Two cameras record the interaction: one on the wrist and one at the robot’s base, rendered in MuJoCo. Using the simulator’s geometry, object poses, and camera information, we calculate each point’s position and visibility in every frame without human annotation and filter out static points on the background and the robot’s fixed base. The pipeline produces RoboTrack-15M for training. RoboTrack-15M has 3,000 videos from 300 simulated homes with 5,000 tracks per video, for 15 million tracks in total. buffer.title: How to build and maintain an agentic evaluation
buffer.text: How to build and maintain an agentic evaluation Back to Articles How to build and maintain an agentic evaluation Published November 23, 2026 Update on GitHub Upvote 31 +25 Avijit Ghosh evijit Follow ben burtenshaw burtenshaw Follow Irene Solaiman irenesolaiman Follow Overview AI evaluations help shape which systems people build, adopt, and trust. An evaluation gives a system tasks, checks its answers or actions, and produces a score. Building and maintaining a useful evaluation therefore takes real work: defining tasks that reflect domain expertise, scoring them reliably, and checking that the results support the claims made. When methods, code, and data stay private, that work is harder for others to scrutinize or build on. Open source offers a means to build stronger, more frequently updated, and more comparable evaluations and the infrastructure around them. Existing tasks, environments, and tools give builders a starting point, so their effort can go to domain expertise and validation. Sharing how an evaluation was built, including what went wrong, lets others find errors, improve it, and reuse it. The Hugging Face hub is the home for AI evaluation: we host around 3500 eval leaderboards and have seen about a 16X growth in eval datasets on the hub in the past year , to about 17000 datasets. In recent months, we have also incorporated support for agentic abstractions that are relevant to evaluation. For example, Traces that store an agent’s work in an easily reviewable and sharable way; Benchmarks that highlight datasets used to evaluate models with leaderboards; and Environments that show datasets used as agentic RL or evaluation environments. This guide covers four things: Three eras of evaluation (section 1). Evaluations moved from checking answers, to checking what an agent did, to checking what a team of agents produces. Each step adds software that can change the score. The steps in an agentic evaluation (section 2). We follow one task through eight steps, from the claim to the reported score. The full walkthrough, with commands, is in Appendix A . When a benchmark is wrong (section 3). Errors in tasks and graders are common. We look at how they are found and corrected. What to open strategically and why (section 4). A table sets out, component by component, what to share and what can stay protected. In the research community, AI evaluation terminology is notoriously inconsistent . The glossary at the end defines each term we use and notes the other names you may come across. 1. Introduction: how evaluation design has changed AI evaluation design has evolved in three forms as language models have become more capable and able to perform more complex work: question answer, agentic, and teams or swarms. Question-answer benchmarks such as MMLU (2020) and GPQA (2023) measure knowledge and reasoning through the answers models produce. As models became capable of planning and using tools, agentic benchmarks such as SWE-bench and WebArena expanded the scope to resolving software issues and completing tasks on websites. These tasks require evaluation setups that account for the environment in which the system operates and the changes it makes. Lately, research on multi-agent systems has started to add another dimension: how agents coordinate and what they accomplish together. This includes decentralized swarms , teams managed by an orchestrator , and specialized agents collaborating on scientific work . Figure 1 shows a rough timeline of these three eras of evaluations. Figure 1. Three types of language model evals. Question-and-answer benchmarks check a response against a key. Agentic benchmarks check what an agent changed in an environment. Team and swarm benchmarks score what a group of agents produced. We’ll focus on agentic evaluations in this article for two reasons. First, they are becoming increasingly the most prominent type in model release announcements due to high user and enterprise interest in agentic deployment. Second, they offer a useful starting point for understanding how evaluation design affects model performance. Team and swarm evaluations introduce further complexity through interactions between agents, which we leave outside the scope of this guide. Once an agent uses tools to complete a task, each part of the surrounding software can affect its score. For instance, in an audit of Terminal-Bench , researchers kept the model fixed and changed the agent harness. Accuracy varied by up to 29.9 percentage points. To understand differences like that, we examine the anatomy of an agentic evaluation and follow one task from the instructions the agent receives to the checks that determine whether it passed. The anatomy of an agentic evaluation Figure 2. The different components of an agentic evaluation. There are various parts to an agentic evaluation. A task gives the agent its instruction. The agent harness wraps the model and its tools, letting it work inside a pinned environment. During one rollout, the agent attempts the task from start to finish: it may run several commands, inspect their output, and try again before it stops. The evaluation harness runs several rollouts for each task. When a rollout ends, the verifier grades the environment's final state. Each rollout also leaves a trace, and traces and scores together become part of the final published evidence. Each part can be published, inspected, and reused separately. Why benchmark release decisions matter Demand for independent evaluation is growing. Policymakers, enterprises, and researchers want evaluations they can verify, and today they mostly cannot: 98.2% of model-benchmark scores are reported by only one party , and researchers have argued that in-house evaluation is not enough . At the same time, more benchmarks are holding back test items to reduce contamination: questions or solutions entering training data, so scores may reflect prior exposure. Artificial Analysis says 60% of its Intelligence Index v5 , announced in October 2026, rests on evaluations with private test sets or held-out answers. Google DeepMind recently piloted double-blind evaluations , where a secure enclave hides an outside evaluator's test prompts from the model provider and the model's weights from the evaluator. While that can reduce contamination, privacy by itself does not guarantee quality, and withholding supporting materials can make expert review harder. We argue that builders can and should still share infrastructure, grading methods, and evidence about task design. Scrutiny depends on giving others a way to question the measurement and correct mistakes, including controlled review where public release is unsuitable. 2. Building an eval: what to reuse, adapt, and validate With the anatomy in place, we now build one agentic evaluation for a real use case: an agent that analyzes measurements for a physics lab. Rather than starting from scratch, we adapt an open task, so most of our effort goes into domain expertise and validation. We work through eight steps: define the claim , find a task , run it unchanged , adapt it , check the evaluation , read the traces , report the score , and compare models . We then take stock of what we reused. The full walkthrough is in Appendix A . Figure 3 maps the steps and what each produced in our example. Figure 3. The eight steps of building an agentic evaluation. The left panel highlights each step in turn, and the right panel shows what it involved in our example. Yellow steps work on the evaluation itself, and orange steps run models and read the results. Method Claim. Consider a physics lab that wants an agent to fit peaks in a Raman spectrum. A Raman spectrum is a measurement whose peaks reveal properties of a material, here graphene. The agent's job is ordinary coding: read the data file, fit a curve to each peak, and save the results (Figure 5 in Appendix A). For the purposes of this article, our claim is deliberately narrow: fit the specified peaks, calculate the requested D-to-G ratio (the intensity of one peak relative to another, which can indicate defects in the material; we also call it the defect ratio), and save accurate results consistently. Reviewing a whole lab report would need additional skills and evidence. Starting task and baseline. We reused the Harbor task format and Terminal-Bench's raman-fitting task. Harbor is an open source evaluation harness, and Terminal-Bench is an open benchmark of tasks that an agent completes in a terminal. We first ran the task's reference solution, which passed, and then ran the original task three times with Terminus-2 , a terminal agent harness, and gpt-oss-120b , an open-weight model from OpenAI. Harbor ran inside an HF Job, each rollout used its own HF Sandbox, and Inference Providers supplied the model responses. Set up your own free personal ChatGPT on your PC with Unsloth and Inkling or Qwen. It's private, and the whole house can use it. By Jerry James · Nov 22, 2026 With the launch of open-weight models like Qwen, cloud-based LLM providers seem like they're more of infrastructure or appliance businesses when it comes to most routine tasks that an AI model can handle. OpenAI and Anthropic have displayed a pattern of dropping model quality in the 'latest' version and controlling exactly what you're allowed to run on their models. Add to this ballooning costs and privacy concerns, and we get a pretty good case for moving away from this 'convenient' cloud experience. That's basically where I was too. I wanted to offload certain token-heavy research, data collection, or coding tasks to an AI model without staring at usage limits all day. So, as any reasonable human being would do, I decided to set up my own local AI : a Claude and ChatGPT replacement that runs at home on my own hardware. Since this was my first attempt, my primary focus was keeping it simple and hosting it on Windows. If you're a beginner, you can follow along to get one going on your home network too. Once you have the hardware sorted, it takes about 10-15 minutes (excluding download times). The short version Install Unsloth Desktop, download a quantized AI model that fits your GPU's VRAM, set your context size, and turn on LAN access so everyone at home can use it. What Do You Need to Run a Local AI at Home? Not much (other than the hardware). Here's a short list: A Windows PC with a graphics card (GPU). The more video memory (VRAM) it has, the bigger the model it can run. I'm using an RTX 5090 with 32GB VRAM for this setup. Unsloth Desktop. A free app that 'serves' the AI model to you through a chat interface. Get it from Unsloth . An AI model sized to fit your GPU. We'll pick one in the next section. That's it. No terminal commands, Python environments, or subscriptions required. Which AI Model Can Your GPU Run? It depends on how much VRAM your graphics card has. As a rough guide, 8-12GB of VRAM handles smaller 9B-12B models, while 32GB comfortably runs 27B-35B models with plenty of room for long conversations. On consumer-grade hardware, we'll need smaller models. The full-size Qwen model sits at around 56GB and won't really fit on a consumer graphics card unless you're running a Mac with unified memory. That's where quantization comes in. What Is Quantization? Quantization shrinks a model by compressing weights and moving to a lower precision. You basically trade some accuracy for a model that actually fits on your GPU and runs faster. The same photo stored at 8, 4 and 2 bits per pixel. A model's weights lose detail the same way going from Q8 to Q4 to Q2. If you're wondering whether this tradeoff is worth it, well, it depends. You'll find that certain types of workloads don't really care and give similar outputs, while others may be nearly unusable. Which Model Should You Run for Your VRAM? For this guide, we'll be going with Qwen3.8-27B with 4-bit quantization on my system with an RTX 5090. Going up a tier is an option thanks to its 32GB of VRAM, but I wanted to allow for a larger context window (how much of the conversation the model can keep in mind at once) rather than cramming in the largest model that fits. Qwen3.8-27B at each precision with a 128K context, from our VRAM calculator . At 4-bit, the model and the context fit a 32 GB card with room to spare. If you want to run a model of this caliber with excellent performance, a hilariously overpriced RTX 5090 (remember when $1,999 felt too high?) is unfortunately still not a terrible 'deal' these days. The other option is way more expensive enterprise-grade GPUs . If you're on a GPU with less VRAM, you can still get something very usable going right away. The core idea: deploy temporary shields against exploits without needing system restarts while waiting on real patches.

Codex even generated a shield to block Java4Shell. Ngl this is clever.

- Uses TPM for hardware-backed verification
- Open-source under BSD 2-Clause license
- Built to let AI agents identify and block emerging threats at machine speed
496289579.source: OpenAI and Cisco launched Shirudo, an open-source runtime for Linux security. Shirudo uses eBPF technology to protect systems without requiring restarts. The tool allows security teams to deploy temporary shields while waiting for permanent patches. Shields are cryptographically signed and verified before being loaded. Shirudo utilizes Trusted Platform Module (TPM) for hardware-backed verification. OpenAI's Codex was used to generate a shield for the Java4Shell exploit. The project is licensed under BSD 2-Clause and dual-licensed BPF programs. Shirudo aims to enable AI agents to identify and protect systems against emerging threats. OpenAI and Cisco introduce Shirudo | OpenAI OpenAI November 23, 2026 Security OpenAI and Cisco introduce Shirudo An open-source runtime that helps operators protect running Linux systems without needing to wait for the patch or restarts Share OpenAI and Cisco are launching Shirudo, an open-source runtime that helps teams protect Linux systems while they roll out patches. In a controlled test ⁠ (opens in a new window) , a Codex-generated shield blocked a Java4Shell exploit attempt against a running Elasticsearch service without requiring a restart. We’re inviting developers, security researchers, and infrastructure operators across the industry to help develop the project further. The project brings together OpenAI’s frontier AI, security and infrastructure research and Cisco’s infrastructure and security expertise to help protect the systems people rely on every day. Testing and deploying a patch can still take days or weeks. Protecting a service in the meantime can be challenging because an exploit and a legitimate request may rely on the same Linux operation. Blocking that operation entirely could take the service offline. Shirudo (Japanese for “shield”) is designed to help security teams navigate this tradeoff. Teams can test whether a temporary safeguard, called a shield, blocks the behavior that exposes a vulnerability while allowing legitimate requests through. Once an operator approves the shield, it can be deployed while the service continues running. “ We’re giving defenders better models and tools to find and fix vulnerabilities faster, but finding a bug today doesn’t mean you can patch every system tomorrow. We are partnering closely with Cisco on Shirudo to help teams protect the systems they need to keep running while they build and roll out a fix. So many teams rely on the same software that it makes sense to build these tools in the open. Now when one team finds a better way to protect a system, others don’t have to start from scratch. ” Greg Brockman, President and Co-founder of OpenAI How Shirudo works Shirudo uses eBPF, a Linux technology that allows small programs to run at specific points inside the operating system. This makes it possible to observe suspicious activity and apply targeted security protections to running systems. How the guardian agent observes and protects a running system with eBPF. OpenAI and Cisco are designing Shirudo around four core capabilities: Live protection: eBPF shields can block vulnerable code paths without restarting the system. Security teams can monitor how a proposed shield would affect applications before enforcing it. Defense at machine speed: OpenAI and Cisco are designing Shirudo to give agents programmable controls to investigate vulnerabilities, develop targeted shields, and validate their effectiveness against exploits and real workloads. Security teams control what gets deployed. Trusted deployment: Shields are cryptographically signed and verified before loading. Linux's eBPF verifier checks eBPF programs against its safety rules, while kernel security controls restrict unauthorized changes. Hardware-backed verification: Shirudo uses a Trusted Platform Module (TPM) to support a verifiable record of protections being loaded or removed. Operators can use this evidence to check whether systems meet their security requirements. The Shirudo technical walkthrough ⁠ (opens in a new window) from the Linux Plumbers Conference shows how to apply a shield and verify it on the target host ⁠ (opens in a new window) . The Java4Shell vulnerability is another example illustrating how a targeted shield can protect a running application while a permanent patch is being prepared. Using OpenAI's Codex, the team generated a shield that added an input check to Java's Base64 decoder and attached it directly to a running Elasticsearch process. When attempting to exploit the vulnerability, the shield rejected the malicious input, blocking the attack while Elasticsearch continued running. You can read more here ⁠ (opens in a new window) . Rethinking infrastructure Shirudo is a first step toward infrastructure that can adapt to emerging threats while remaining reliable.
